newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FOCUS-AUSTRALIA PLANS MASSIVE TAX OVERHAUL.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-AUSTRALIA PLANS MASSIVE TAX OVERHAUL.

text.p: Australia's conservative government on Wednesday stepped up its campaign for tax reform, vowing to cut income taxes and pledging to declare its plans ahead of the next election.
Prime Minister John Howard said his Liberal-National coalition would consider a new broad-based indirect tax to replace existing levies and fund a cut to income taxes.
"The coalition will have a plan to take Australia into the 21st century with a modern, fairer, better tax system," he said.
Howard said he was not committed to a particular blueprint for tax reform and repeated earlier assurances not to introduce new taxes in the government's first three-year term, due to end by mid-1999.
He said the government will set up a reform taskforce,

"I want to make it very clear to you that I have a strong personal commitment to taxation reform, that I have a very clear view of the directions that I would like to go in reforming the Australian taxation system," Howard said.

"We need a taxation system that gives incentives to ordinary Australians to save, to invest, to take risks. We need a taxation system that promotes job generation. We need a taxation system that helps rather than hinders exports."

The coalition has long favoured a tax on consumption of goods and services, but abandoned that policy in its successful 1996 election campaign after losing what was regarded as an unloseable election in 1993 with a policy for such a tax.

Business and community groups have stepped up their calls for reforms to Australia's tax system, with its near 50 percent top income tax and a complex and patchy range of indirect taxes. Howard said there was strong support within the government for reform and challenged the Labor opposition to back the push for change and avoid running a fear campaign at the next election.

"Anybody who has the national economic interest at heart knows that we cannot go into the 21st century with our existing taxation system," he said. Labor has spoken out against any move to introduce a goods and services tax (GST).
Howard did not say when the taskforce -- made up of senior officials from his department and Treasury -- would report to the government, but pledged widespread community consultation.
"The Australian public will have a very clear idea of where we intend to go," he said.

Howard also said the government's reforms would include a revamp of the financial relations with Australia's six states and two territories, would not increase the total tax take and would compensate the poor if they were disadvantaged by the changes.
